text: The REST Message record is the real ServiceNow object for calling an external REST API outbound. It lives in the sys_rest_message table, and it's the starting point for every outbound integration this chapter covers — before any script exists, this record is where the connection itself gets defined.

The parent REST Message record holds two things at that top level: a base Endpoint, like the weather service's root URL, and a default Authentication Profile that every operation underneath it inherits automatically. Rotate the credential once on the parent, and every child operation picks up the fix without you touching anything else.

The parent can't send anything by itself, though — it has no HTTP method and no path of its own. Each real operation is a separate child record called a REST Message Function, with its own HTTP method, its own relative path appended to the base Endpoint, and its own headers and body. A getCurrentConditions GET and a getForecast GET can live side by side under the same parent, each with its own placeholder syntax like dollar-sign curly-brace city, filled in by script later in Lesson 6.

This split exists because real external APIs are organized the same way: one host, many endpoints hanging off it. Reusing the Authentication Profile across every Function avoids re-entering credentials for each operation, and calling code only ever needs two strings to reach any configured operation — the REST Message name and the Function name, nothing more.

Don't confuse this with the Scripted REST APIs coming in Chapter 4. A REST Message is outbound — ServiceNow calling someone else's system. A Scripted REST API is inbound — someone else calling into ServiceNow. Same HTTP concepts, same methods and headers and JSON bodies, but opposite direction, and genuinely different records under the hood.

Parent record, base connection, configured once. Child record, one operation each, as many as you actually need. Next up: actually building a REST Message and testing a Function's real response before you ever touch a line of script.
